name: Hair Dryer
blurb: Hair dryers pull 1,500–1,875 watts — as much as a space heater — but only for minutes at a time. Daily ten-minute drying works out to roughly a dollar a month even in high-rate states.

name: Flat Iron / Hair Straightener
blurb: Flat irons hold temperature with 50–200 watts across small plates. Regular styling costs a few cents a month; forgetting one on is a fire question, not a bill question.

name: Curling Iron
blurb: Curling irons draw well under 150 watts for short sessions — electricity is the cheapest part of any hair routine.

name: Electric Shaver
blurb: Shavers charge tiny batteries and draw single-digit watts. A year of daily shaving uses less electricity than one load in an electric dryer.

name: Electric Toothbrush
blurb: An electric toothbrush on its charging stand consumes on the order of 1–2 kWh per year — a dime or two. Inductive stands left plugged in draw fractions of a watt on modern models.

name: Towel Warmer
blurb: Heated towel racks draw 60–250 watts, and the habit that matters is runtime: on a timer for an hour before showers, cost is trivial; left on 24/7, a large rack rivals a refrigerator.

name: Bathroom Exhaust Fan
blurb: Bath fans draw 15–60 watts. Running one for 20 minutes after showers costs almost nothing and prevents the mold and moisture damage that actually gets expensive — but in winter, every hour it runs also exhausts air your heater already paid to warm.

name: CPAP Machine
blurb: A CPAP with a heated humidifier draws 30–90 watts through the night, totaling a modest few kilowatt-hours a month. The humidifier and heated hose account for most of the draw — the blower itself uses very little.
tips: Humidifier and heated-hose settings drive most of the power — use the lowest comfortable levels.
For camping or backup batteries, disabling humidification triples runtime.
A dedicated CPAP battery sized around 90 Wh typically covers one night without humidification.

name: Oxygen Concentrator
blurb: Home oxygen concentrators draw 300–600 watts and often run continuously — a genuine, unavoidable 200+ kWh a month for many users. Some states and utilities offer medical-equipment rate discounts; anyone running one around the clock should ask their utility about them.
tips: Ask your utility about medical baseline or life-support rate programs — many offer real discounts.
Portable units on battery use far less power but deliver lower flow; sizing matters medically, so change nothing without your provider.
Keep filters clean — restricted intake raises power draw and wears the compressor.

name: Tanning Bed (Home)
blurb: Home tanning beds run banks of lamps totaling 1,500–5,000 watts. Sessions are short, so cost per session is modest — the fixed price of the habit is in bulbs, not kilowatt-hours.

name: Light Therapy (SAD) Lamp
blurb: A 10,000-lux therapy lamp draws 20–75 watts for a typical 30-minute morning session. An entire winter of daily use costs less than a single latte.

name: Massage Chair
blurb: Massage chairs draw 60–300 watts mid-program, with heating features at the top end. Daily sessions add up to a dollar or two monthly — check standby draw, since some models idle at 10+ watts.

name: Heated Bidet Seat
blurb: Heated bidet seats keep the seat warm and heat water on demand, effectively averaging 30–60 watts continuously. Eco or timer modes that let the seat cool overnight cut consumption roughly in half.
